content: This initiative was presented at the 10th International AIDS Society Conference held in Mexico City in July 2019. In Burundi, peer providers played a critical role in supporting individuals from HIV self-testing to ART initiation. This approach was also discussed at the same conference in 2019. A community-based ART delivery model was developed for female sex workers in Tanzania, with baseline findings published in AIDS Care in 2019. Additionally, a six-month evaluation of ART initiation and adherence among this population was detailed in AIDS Behavior the same year. Patient navigators have been systematically reviewed as an effective strategy for supporting individuals with chronic diseases, including HIV, as published in PloS One in 2018. Similarly, interventions to improve linkage to and retention in pre-ART care in lowand middle-income settings were systematically reviewed in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2014. The role of people living with HIV/AIDS as peers in improving engagement in the HIV care cascade was systematically reviewed in AIDS Behavior in 2016. This highlighted the importance of peer involvement in care delivery. In Zambia, community-based assisted HIV self-testing among youth was evaluated for its cost and impact at the 2019 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle. Similarly, in Eswatini, peer-delivered linkage case management and same-day ART initiation for men and young people with HIV were implemented between 2015 and 2017, as reported in the MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report in 2018. In Lesotho, the CASCADE randomized clinical trial compared same-day ART initiation during home-based HIV testing to usual health facility referrals. The results, published in JAMA in 2018, demonstrated improved linkage to care and viral suppression. A similar trial in Malawi, published in JAMA in 2014, evaluated the effect of optional home initiation of HIV care following self-testing on ART initiation. The World Health Organization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of demand creation strategies to improve HIV testing uptake, as outlined in a 2019 report. A paradigm shift focusing on the HIV prevention continuum was also discussed in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2014. The 2019 WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services (HTS) stress the need to focus on undiagnosed individuals with HIV and link them to treatment and care as early as possible. HIV-negative individuals at ongoing risk should also be tested and connected to prevention services. Differentiated HTS approaches, including facility-based, community-based, and HIV self-testing (HIVST), are recommended to address specific epidemiological and resource contexts. Integration of HTS with other health services, such as tuberculosis (TB), viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and reproductive health, is prioritized to minimize missed opportunities for testing. Task sharing and the use of trained lay providers are recommended to expand HTS, particularly in community-based settings. Lay providers, including peers, can deliver non-judgmental and respectful services, improving uptake and linkage to care. The test for triage approach, where a single HIV rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is performed by a trained provider, facilitates linkage to further testing and services. This strategy supports community-based HTS and HIVST, ensuring individuals with reactive results receive confirmatory testing and appropriate care. Facility-based HTS, including routine testing in clinical settings, has proven effective in increasing coverage and normalizing HIV testing. In high HIV burden settings, routine testing is recommended for all clients, while in low burden settings, it should focus on key populations and individuals with HIV-related conditions. Integration of HTS into antenatal care (ANC) has achieved high testing coverage among pregnant women in high HIV burden settings. Dual HIV/syphilis RDTs are recommended to address gaps in syphilis testing and treatment. Similarly, integrating HTS with family planning services can address the needs of sexually active adolescents and young women. Routine HTS is also recommended for infants and children with unknown HIV status in high burden settings, as well as for clients with presumptive or confirmed TB. Early detection and linkage to TB treatment alongside ART can prevent deaths among people with HIV. Clinical and prevention services for key populations, such as harm reduction services for people who inject drugs, provide important entry points for HTS. Routine HTS in STI clinics and viral hepatitis services is also recommended, given the high rates of co-infection. Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) services in high HIV burden countries include HTS as part of their delivery. Addressing structural and policy barriers, such as age of consent laws, is essential to improve HTS uptake in these settings. Finally, HTS should be routinely offered in inpatient, outpatient, and emergency hospital settings to clients with symptoms or conditions indicative of HIV. Risk-based screening tools may help increase coverage in low burden settings, provided they are validated and implemented appropriately.
